displayQuote: Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!

meta.title: Who really said "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Verified: Ronald Reagan said it at the Brandenburg Gate on 12 June 1987. The official text, his own reading copy, and the fight to keep the line in.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!'?
meta.ogDescription: Reagan really said it — Brandenburg Gate, 12 June 1987. Speechwriter Peter Robinson drafted it; State and the NSC tried seven times to cut it.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Reagan said it at the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin on 12 June 1987, near the end of his “Remarks on East-West Relations.” The sentence stands word for word in the official text released by the U.S. government and in the President’s own typed backup reading copy held by the Reagan Library.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Remarks on East-West Relations at the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin
12 June 1987, 2:20 p.m., Brandenburg Gate, West Berlin
Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: Ronald Reagan, 1987, Book I, 634–637

source.excerpt: There is one sign the Soviets can make that would be unmistakable, that would advance dramatically the cause of freedom and peace. General Secretary Gorbachev, if you seek peace, if you seek prosperity for the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, if you seek liberalization: Come here to this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!
trail: The Reagan Library’s text of the remarks ↗ carries the sentence and notes that the President spoke at 2:20 p.m. at the Brandenburg Gate on 12 June 1987.

The State Department’s Foreign Relations of the United States series ↗ reprints the speech and gives its source as Public Papers: Reagan, 1987, Book I, pp. 634–637; the American Presidency Project ↗ prints the same wording.
Speechwriter Peter Robinson traces the passage to a West Berlin dinner where Ingeborg Elz said of Gorbachev, “He can get rid of this Wall” — his account is at the Hoover Institution ↗.

State and the NSC sent seven alternative drafts stripped of the challenge; per Robinson’s Prologue article ↗, deputy chief of staff Kenneth Duberstein recalled Reagan smiling and saying, “Let’s leave it in.”
source.excerptNote: The famous sentence is the last of three imperatives. In the President’s typed reading copy each stands alone on its own line, in capitals, ending with a period rather than the exclamation mark of the published text.

author.name: Ronald Reagan
author.heading: About Ronald Reagan
author.metaLine: 1911–2004 · 40th U.S. President (1981–1989); earlier a film actor and Governor of California
author.bio: Ronald Wilson Reagan was born in Tampico, Illinois, on 6 February 1911 and died in Los Angeles on 5 June 2004. He acted in Hollywood films, led the Screen Actors Guild, and served as Governor of California from 1967 to 1975 before winning the presidency in 1980. His Cold War rhetoric — delivered with an actor’s timing and defended against his own advisers — produced the single most quoted sentence of his eight years in office.

misattribution.heading: What gets muddled
misattribution.intro: The attribution itself is not in doubt — Reagan said these words, on camera, in front of the Wall. What gets muddled is who wrote them, what the sentence actually accomplished, and which demonstrative it uses.

items.who: Peter Robinson drafted the line — and Reagan’s chief speechwriter later claimed otherwise
items.why: Robinson has described writing the passage in his own National Archives account ↗, and the President’s backup reading copy is headed “(ROBINSON).” Chief speechwriter Anthony Dolan later published a Wall Street Journal article in November 2009 arguing that Reagan produced the line himself in an Oval Office meeting before Robinson’s draft, which prompted a published exchange of letters between the two men ↗. Either way, Reagan chose to say it over his advisers’ objections.

items.who: Not the speech that opened the Wall
items.why: The address drew little notice at the time; TASS called it “openly provocative, war-mongering,” and the senior U.S. diplomat in Berlin, John Kornblum, said it “wasn’t really elevated to its current status until 1989, after the wall came down” (Wikipedia’s survey of the reception ↗). The Wall opened on 9 November 1989 ↗.

The demonstrative slips easily — Robinson titled his own Hoover Institution essay “Tearing Down That Wall” ↗. The delivered text reads “this wall,” paired with the line before it, “Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate!”, because Reagan was standing at the gate and in front of the Wall.

misattribution.truthLine: Reagan said it, in these words, at the Brandenburg Gate on 12 June 1987 — the official text ↗ and his own reading copy both carry the sentence.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line began at a dinner table, not a desk. Speechwriter Peter Robinson went to West Berlin ahead of the trip and asked his hosts whether they had gotten used to the Wall; Ingeborg Elz answered that if Gorbachev were serious about glasnost and perestroika, “he can prove it. He can get rid of this Wall.” Robinson took the thought home and turned it into three hammer-blow imperatives: come here to this gate, open this gate, tear down this wall.

Then his own government tried to delete it. By Robinson’s account the State Department and the National Security Council fought the passage for weeks, calling it naïve, needlessly provocative and a cruel gimmick that would raise Berliners’ hopes, and sent over no fewer than seven alternative drafts — one offering only that “one day, this ugly wall will disappear.” Reagan kept his version. Deputy chief of staff Kenneth Duberstein remembered the President smiling and saying, “Let’s leave it in.”
detailsBody: The speech was not an instant sensation. Coverage at the time was thin, and the Soviet press agency TASS called it an “openly provocative, war-mongering speech.” The senior American diplomat in Berlin, John Kornblum, later said the address “wasn’t really elevated to its current status until 1989, after the wall came down.”

The Berlin Wall opened on 9 November 1989, when, in the State Department historian’s words, “thousands of jubilant Germans brought down the most visible symbol of division at the heart of Europe.” Reagan had left office ten months earlier; the sentence he insisted on keeping became the epitaph for the Wall rather than the cause of its fall.
context.pull: The boys at State are going to kill me, but it’s the right thing to do.
